endorsements.quote: AI‐generated outputs should therefore remain advisory, with clinicians retaining responsibility for interpreting recommendations and making final decisions.

AI models developed using datasets from high‐income countries may not perform equally well in the Cambodian population because of differences in disease prevalence, demographic characteristics, imaging equipment, referral patterns, clinical practices, and data quality.
Prospective studies should therefore evaluate AI systems under real‐world Cambodian conditions before wider deployment.

Pilot projects should include explicit criteria for continuation, scale‐up, adaptation, or discontinuation rather than being treated as successful solely because technical feasibility has been demonstrated.
Local and prospective validation should assess performance across relevant populations and healthcare settings, with continued monitoring after deployment.

Clear governance should therefore define who is responsible for AI‐supported decisions, how systems are validated and approved, how adverse events are monitored, and what processes exist for auditing and updating models.
Healthcare professionals require practical competencies to understand AI capabilities, limitations, risks, and appropriate use.
AI and digital‐health competencies should be incorporated into continuing professional development and, where appropriate, medical and health‐science curricula.
Transparent communication about the benefits, limitations, privacy implications, and appropriate use of AI can strengthen trust and reduce unrealistic expectations.
AI adoption should therefore be guided by health need, evidence, feasibility, equity, affordability, and sustainability, rather than technological novelty alone.
Locally conducted studies should evaluate diagnostic and clinical performance, usability, equity, cost‐effectiveness, workflow integration, patient outcomes, and sustainability.

A phased approach that combines digital‐health strengthening, local research, economic evaluation, workforce development, ethical governance, and prospective clinical and public health evaluation is therefore warranted.

unlisted_practices: Conduct cost-effectiveness, budget-impact, and opportunity-cost analyses of AI applications before adoption.
Prioritize interoperability and integration of digital health systems rather than creating disconnected platforms.
Engage healthcare professionals, patients, and communities in AI development.
Plan recurrent financing and long-term maintenance for AI initiatives so they remain sustainable after external project support ends.
Build digital infrastructure (connectivity, electricity, secure data infrastructure) as a prerequisite for AI deployment.
Prioritize local ownership and capacity development in international partnerships rather than long-term dependence on external technical support.
Evaluate AI-enabled telemedicine for whether it actually expands access among underserved populations.
